name: yacas
why: A general purpose computer algebra system with its own scripting language, an old-school environment worth exploring.

brief.what_it_is: Yacas (Yet Another Computer Algebra System) is a general-purpose computer algebra system for symbolic manipulation of mathematical expressions. You type infix-notation expressions and it manipulates them symbolically, with arbitrary-precision arithmetic in the core engine. The distribution ships a small library of mathematical functions, but the README says its main strength is the scripting language, where you write your own symbolic manipulation rules and algorithms. It is aimed at mathematicians, engineers, and students, and is usable from a command-line interface.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a free, open-source alternative to commercial CAS software, suitable for research, education, and recreational mathematics. The project's own framing is that it was built for a broad audience, not only specialists.
brief.how_it_works: A parser built on an infix-operator grammar reads expressions. The core engine applies user-defined rules to mathematical objects to carry out symbolic transformations, and it supports arbitrary-precision arithmetic. The README does not go deeper into the internals; the docs index lists a Reference Manual, a Programming in Yacas guide, and a Book of Algorithms, which I did not open.
brief.install_notes: The homepage and README point to a Downloads page (http://www.yacas.org/getting_started/downloads/) for binary packages and installation instructions across platforms. I did not fetch that page, so I have no verified per-platform steps. Nothing in the README mentions accounts, runtimes, or first-run configuration. The brew formula exposes a single executable named yacas.
brief.standout: The scripting language is the point, not the built-in function library: the README says the real strength is in writing your own symbolic manipulation algorithms. It is an older, self-contained, LGPL-licensed CAS with its own language, rather than a wrapper around another system, and it has a browser demo on the homepage (Yacas Online) and a Visual Studio Code syntax highlighting post on the blog.
brief.status: Unknown. The homepage lists release 1.9.1 (also 1.8.0 and 1.7.0) under recent articles, but I saw no release dates. The GitHub repo page I fetched showed CI and coverage badges and an issue tracker and mailing forum, but no commit dates or last-activity information. The docs page I fetched was only a table of contents. The brew description and scout note are consistent with an active, released project, but I could not confirm recency.
brief.caveats: Licensed under the GNU Lesser General Public License v2.1 or later. The README's own intro is somewhat promotional in its "who is yacas for" section (it claims under 1% of the population are math enthusiasts), which is a tone note rather than a limitation. I did not verify platform support beyond the README's statement that it is available for a variety of platforms. The homepage 'More' links for blog articles and release notes were not followed, so release dates and changelog details are missing from these notes.
quotes: Yacas (Yet Another Computer Algebra System) is a small and highly flexible general-purpose Computer Algebra System (CAS).
its real strength is in the language in which you can easily write your own symbolic manipulation algorithms.
it serves as a free alternative to commercial CAS software.
